title: Lock a castle nut with a cotter pin: push it through the slot and the stud's cross-hole, then spread its prongs
instruction: Lock the castle nut with the cotter pin: push it through the nut's slot and the stud's hole, then spread its prongs apart.
context: Automotive service technicians (about 826,000 US jobs, BLS 2025) pin castle nuts when they rebuild steering linkages (O*NET 49-3023.00: "Tear down, repair, and rebuild faulty assemblies, such as power systems, steering systems, and linkages"). Service manuals call for a new pin every time, its prongs bent round the nut (Suzuki RA410: "bend new split pin"): an unpinned tie-rod nut can work loose and the steering with it. The work is physical: a 2.2 mm pin has to go in square through a 3.0 mm hole hidden under the nut's slot, between the steering arm, the knuckle and the tie rod; its prongs lie together, so the end where the longer one runs on past the shorter has to be caught first; each prong takes about 12 N, 10 mm from its root, to bend; and meanwhile the pin's head has to be held home.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left); heights above the table top. Steering joint (wheel off) on a steel stand 16.5 x 20 x 5 cm (x 27.5 to 44.0, y -8.5 to 11.5): a steel steering arm 3.4 cm wide and 1.4 cm thick, its top 9.0 cm up, running from the knuckle body (x 40.0 to 42.5, 6 cm wide, 8.5 cm tall) to just past an upright 3/8-24 tie-rod-end stud (9.5 mm) at (30.0, 0.0); under the arm round the stud, the ball housing (3.2 cm across) and its rubber boot, the tie rod (1.8 cm thick) running off to y 11.0; beyond the knuckle, the brake dust shield (x 43.0, 16 cm wide, 11 cm tall). On the arm, round the stud: a zinc-plated 3/8-24 slotted hex nut, 9/16 in (14.3 mm) across flats, flats facing front and back, 8.3 mm thick, six slots 3.2 mm wide and 3.2 mm deep, one running front to back over the stud's 3.0 mm cross-hole (its centre 9.7 cm up). Cotter pin: a new standard 3/32 x 1 in low-carbon steel extended-prong cotter pin (ASME B18.8.1): half-round prongs 1.1 x 2.2 mm lying together, 25.4 mm from under the eye to the short prong's end, the other prong 4 mm longer, eye 6 mm across, about 1.4 g; it lies flat in a groove 3.0 mm wide and 1.0 mm deep along the top of an aluminium block 6 x 2 x 2 cm (x 24.6 to 30.6, centred on y -18.0), prongs pointing at the robot, the eye and 8 mm of shank sticking out past the block's far end (the eye's centre at (31.7, -18.0)). Screwdriver: a precision flat-head 120 mm long, 30 g: a steel blade 2.5 x 0.4 mm for its first 8 mm, widening evenly to 4 x 3 mm 40 mm up, then a red plastic handle 18 mm square and 80 mm long; it stands tip down in a grey plastic rack (a 3 x 3 cm block 2.8 cm tall with a 4 mm square hole) centred at (22.0, 18.0).
scoring: Tools: a phone camera held straight above the nut, a protractor and a 1 mm feeler gauge. Through: the pin passes through the stud's cross-hole along the slot (its axis within 15 degrees of the slot's), the prongs' roots out past the stud. Prong angle: in the photo, the angle between the pin's axis and a line from the prong's root, where it leaves the nut, to its tip, counted outwards; the prongs are that far apart in all (the sum of the two). Home: the feeler gauge does not go in between the pin's eye and the nut. At the end: 0 if the pin is not through; 0.25 through, the prongs less than 45 degrees apart; 0.5 at least 45 but less than 90 degrees apart, or one prong less than 30 degrees out; 0.75 at least 90 degrees apart and each prong at least 30 degrees out, but the eye not home, or the robot touching the pin, or the screwdriver's tip within 2 cm of the prongs' roots; 1.0 the same with the eye home, the robot off the pin and the screwdriver away, held for 1 s.
reset_notes: A spread cotter pin is not reused: each trial takes a new straight pin, laid in the block's groove as in the setup. Stand the screwdriver back in its rack.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX, 20 Hz control. The nut, stud, pin and screwdriver have standard sizes, the steering joint's parts a car's, and the pin the mass of steel. Each prong is hinged where it leaves the nut: elastic up to the plastic moment of its low-carbon steel wire (118 N mm, about 12 N at 10 mm), then it keeps its bend less a 2 degree springback, so pushing a prong round takes about the real force. Contacts are rigid.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (3,600 steps; the right arm hovered over the pin in its block but never took hold of it; the left arm reached towards the screwdriver in its rack and drew back without picking it up; the pin and the screwdriver never moved); demo: 1.0 (reached at 68 s, about 1,350 steps)
